y-m-78-01.title: Two box plots: can we say A is faster?
y-m-78-01.topic: Comparing two groups with box plots: overlap and what can be read
y-m-78-01.goal: Tell apart what can and cannot be read for certain from a box plot, and look together at a small difference in medians, the overlap of the boxes, and the amount of data to decide how confident to be in a judgment.
y-m-78-01.material:
Two local snack shops, A and B, published the delivery times (from order to arrival, in minutes) of their recent orders as box plots. Described in words, the box plots are as follows.

| | Minimum | First quartile | Median | Third quartile | Maximum |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 15 | 23 | 28 | 38 | 55 |
| B | 20 | 26 | 31 | 40 | 52 |

(The first quartile is the value where the smaller quarter ends, and the third quartile is the value where the larger quarter starts. The box covers the values between the first and third quartiles, that is, the middle half of the data.) Shorter delivery time is better. The person in charge at the delivery app wants to label A as 'the faster shop'.
y-m-78-01.thinking.0: Comparing the difference in medians and the length of the box (how spread out) together
y-m-78-01.thinking.1: Sorting out what can and cannot be known from the box plot alone
y-m-78-01.thinking.2: Checking your judgment and confidence after learning the amount of data
y-m-78-01.prereq.0: This task is at the 'H1' difficulty (introductory high school level) in this platform's production allocation, and it does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this subject to a particular grade. Assume you already know the prerequisite concepts below.
y-m-78-01.prereq.1: How to read the minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, and maximum from a box plot
y-m-78-01.prereq.2: The median is the middle value when the data is arranged in order of size
y-m-78-01.s.s1.prompt: Based on the box plots alone, first judge whether the person in charge may label A as 'the faster shop'. Which is the most fitting?
y-m-78-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write the numbers for the range where the two boxes overlap.
y-m-78-01.s.s1.hint.1: Find the difference in medians (minutes) and the length of the box (minutes) and compare them with each other.
y-m-78-01.s.s1.o.a: A's median is smaller, so every one of A's orders arrives faster than B's orders, without exception.
y-m-78-01.s.s1.r.a: The median is just one middle value. It does not compare all the values of the two groups. A's maximum of 55 is greater than B's maximum of 52.
y-m-78-01.s.s1.o.b: The two boxes are about the same length, so the delivery times of the two shops are completely the same.
y-m-78-01.s.s1.r.b: It is true that the box lengths (about 15 minutes and 14 minutes) are similar, but that does not erase the fact that the medians differ by 3 minutes. 'Completely the same' is also too strong a statement.
y-m-78-01.s.s1.o.c: The medians differ by only 3 minutes, and the boxes overlap a lot, so it is not a clear difference.
y-m-78-01.s.s1.r.c: You looked at the small difference in medians together with the overlap of the middle half of the data. There is a tendency in one direction, but you were careful about how large the difference is.
y-m-78-01.s.s1.o.d: B's fastest order is 20 minutes, which is slower, so B's delivery time is more stable.
y-m-78-01.s.s1.r.d: One fastest order does not tell stability. Stability should be seen by how spread out the data is (the box length, the overall range).
y-m-78-01.s.s1.explain: The two boxes overlap heavily in the range of about 26 to 38 minutes. A's median being 3 minutes smaller is only a hint of 'a tendency for A to be slightly faster', and does not mean that all orders or most orders are faster at A.
y-m-78-01.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the things that 'can be known' from this box plot alone.
y-m-78-01.s.s2.hint.0: Find out which of the five numbers of the box plot each choice comes from.
y-m-78-01.s.s2.hint.1: Look at whether choices are mixed in that cannot be said from those values alone (counts, weather, and so on).
y-m-78-01.s.s2.o.a: At A, at least half of the orders arrived within 28 minutes.
y-m-78-01.s.s2.r.a: You used the meaning of the median. The values at or below the median are at least half.
y-m-78-01.s.s2.o.b: At B, more than half of the orders arrived within 30 minutes.
y-m-78-01.s.s2.r.b: If B's median is 31, it means at least half of the orders took 31 minutes or more. Then 30 minutes or less cannot be more than half.
y-m-78-01.s.s2.o.c: Which of A and B has more orders.
y-m-78-01.s.s2.r.c: A box plot does not show the number of data values. The count has to be given separately.
y-m-78-01.s.s2.o.d: At B, about a quarter of the orders took 40 minutes or more.
y-m-78-01.s.s2.r.d: You used the meaning of the third quartile. The larger quarter is at or above that value.
y-m-78-01.s.s2.explain: The median means 'at least half are at or below this value', and the third quartile means 'about a quarter are at or above this value'. On the other hand, counts and specific times of day (for example, rainy days) are information that is not in a box plot.
y-m-78-01.s.s3.prompt: There is something new you have learned. The two box plots were each made from only the 'latest 20 orders'. Is your first judgment unchanged, or does it change? Write the reason, and write at least one kind of data you would like to know to make your judgment firmer.
y-m-78-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write your first judgment and the new fact side by side.
y-m-78-01.s.s3.hint.1: Write in one sentence how the amount of data, 20 orders, affects how much you believe the 3-minute difference.
y-m-78-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: My first judgment was ... because ...
y-m-78-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you connect your first judgment with the new fact (if you kept it, why you kept it; if you changed it, what changed)?
y-m-78-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write both the grounds for saying A is faster and the grounds for why it is hard to say so definitely?
y-m-78-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Is the additional data I asked for data that would really help the judgment (for example, more orders, a breakdown by time of day)?
y-m-78-01.s.s3.model.0: My first judgment stays the same. The medians are A 28 minutes and B 31 minutes, only a 3-minute difference, and the boxes overlap a lot. Also, with only 20 orders, a difference like this could be by chance, so I can't say for sure that A is faster. I want to gather more orders and check.
y-m-78-01.s.s3.model.1: I change my judgment a little. Looking at the medians alone, A had a tendency to be faster, but with only 20 orders the data is small, so my confidence dropped. I need data from at least the latest 100 orders for each shop and data by time of day, such as lunch and dinner.
y-m-78-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: Both keeping and revising are valid if there is a reason.

y-m-78-02.title: If the weighting changes, does the ranking change?
y-m-78-02.topic: Weighted average: converted scores that change with the weighting
y-m-78-02.goal: Confirm that the order of two students' converted scores can change depending on the weighting, find several weightings that satisfy all the given conditions, and discuss the fairness of choosing a weighting.
y-m-78-02.material:
A subject's semester grade is found by multiplying the 'written test' and 'performance assessment' scores by set weights and adding them, converted to a score out of 100. If the weight of the written test is p%, the weight of the performance assessment is q%, and p+q=100. Both assessments are out of 100.

| | Written test score | Performance score |
|---|---|---|
| Minseo | 72 | 96 |
| Doyun | 94 | 70 |

Assume the two students' scores do not change. The weights have not been decided yet.
y-m-78-02.thinking.0: Finding several values that satisfy several conditions at the same time
y-m-78-02.thinking.1: Looking at the effect of the weighting on each of the two students separately
y-m-78-02.thinking.2: Evaluating why the criteria must be decided first
y-m-78-02.prereq.0: This task is at the 'H1' difficulty (introductory high school level) in this platform's production allocation, and it does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this subject to a particular grade. Assume you already know the prerequisite concepts below.
y-m-78-02.prereq.1: The meaning of percentages, and calculations with decimals and fractions
y-m-78-02.prereq.2: The fact that a subject's grade is determined by combining several assessment scores at set weights
y-m-78-02.s.s1.prompt: If you raise the weight of the written test (for example, from 40% to 60%), how do you expect the two students' converted scores to change?
y-m-78-02.s.s1.hint.0: Find the converted scores of the two students for p=40 and p=60 and write them side by side.
y-m-78-02.s.s1.hint.1: Look at which way each student's score moves as p gets larger.
y-m-78-02.s.s1.o.a: However the weight of the written test is changed, the order of the two students' converted scores is always the same.
y-m-78-02.s.s1.r.a: For the order to always be the same, one student would have to be higher on both scores. The two students have their high scores on different assessments.
y-m-78-02.s.s1.o.b: If you raise the weight of the written test, both students' converted scores go up.
y-m-78-02.s.s1.r.b: A weighting does not make scores; it changes which score gets more weight. A student with a low score on one side can actually go down.
y-m-78-02.s.s1.o.c: Minseo, who has the larger gap between scores, is always converted higher regardless of the weighting.
y-m-78-02.s.s1.r.c: A large gap between the two scores does not always make the converted score high. What matters is which score gets the weight.
y-m-78-02.s.s1.o.d: If you raise the weight of the written test, Doyun gains and Minseo loses.
y-m-78-02.s.s1.r.d: You pointed out the direction: the student with the higher written score gains and the one with the lower score loses. You can find by calculation from what percent the order actually changes.
y-m-78-02.s.s1.explain: As the written weight p gets larger, Doyun (94), who has the higher written score, gains, and Minseo (96), who has the higher performance score, loses. The p at which the two students' converted scores become equal is about 54.2% (72p+96q=94p+70q, p+q=100).
y-m-78-02.s.s2.prompt:
Enter 2 different weightings that satisfy all of the following conditions. (written p%, performance q%, both integers)
① p+q=100
② Both written and performance are at least 20%
③ Minseo's converted score is at least 85
④ Doyun's converted score is at least 80
y-m-78-02.s.s2.hint.0: First roughly find the range of p that satisfies only ③, then find the range that satisfies only ④, and look at where they overlap.
y-m-78-02.s.s2.hint.1: Pick one p and calculate the two students' converted scores, then change p by 1 and compare which way the scores move.
y-m-78-02.s.s2.fail.c1: The two weights do not add up to 100.
y-m-78-02.s.s2.ok.c2: Each weight is an integer that is at least 20%.
y-m-78-02.s.s2.fail.c2: Each weight must be an integer that is at least 20.
y-m-78-02.s.s2.ok.c3: Minseo's converted score is at least 85.
y-m-78-02.s.s2.fail.c3: Minseo's converted score falls short of 85. (72×p+96×q must be at least 8500)
y-m-78-02.s.s2.ok.c4: Doyun's converted score is at least 80.
y-m-78-02.s.s2.fail.c4: Doyun's converted score falls short of 80. (94×p+70×q must be at least 8000)
y-m-78-02.s.s2.explain: The only integer weightings that satisfy the conditions are written 42% to 45%. If the written weight is 41%, Doyun falls short of 80, and if it is 46%, Minseo falls short of 85. A range that seems possible at first narrows because it works in opposite directions on the two students.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.prompt: Judge whether it is acceptable for a school to set the weights in this way, 'adjusting the weights after seeing the two students' scores'.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.hint.0: Check again where the students' scores were used in ① to ④.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.hint.1: Think about how you must explain when the criteria are set and who they apply to if you want to say a criterion is 'fair'.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.o.a: Choose the weighting after the scores come out so that the student you want gets a high score.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.r.a: If you choose the criteria after seeing the results, the criteria become for a particular student.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.o.b: Decide the weights before the test and apply them equally to all students.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.r.b: You pointed out that the criteria are set before the scores and applied the same to everyone.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.o.c: Apply to each student separately the weighting that gives that student's highest score.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.r.c: If the criteria differ for each student, you can't compare one another's converted scores.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.o.d: The weighting does not affect the converted scores, so it's fine however it is set.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.r.d: As you calculated yourself, the converted scores and the order change depending on the weighting.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.explain: You confirmed that the weighting changes the converted scores and the order. So it has to be set before the scores come out, to fit the goal of the assessment, and applied the same to everyone. In this task, 'finding weightings that satisfy the conditions' was an exercise for understanding how the weighting affects the results.

y-m-78-03.title: A 12-point gap and an 18-point gap: which one is the bigger difference?
y-m-78-03.topic: Comparing scores from different tests using the standard deviation
y-m-78-03.goal: Compare scores from different tests not only by the difference from the mean but also together with how spread out they are (standard deviation), and state the assumptions that make that comparison trustworthy.
y-m-78-03.material:
Hayun got 82 in Korean and 74 in math on the same grade's tests. The results for the whole grade are as follows (all tests are out of 100).

| | Hayun's score | Grade mean | Standard deviation (how spread out the scores are around the mean) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Korean | 82 | 70 | 6 |
| Math | 74 | 56 | 12 |

Hayun thinks, 'In math I'm 18 points above the mean and in Korean 12 points above, so I did better in math.'
y-m-78-03.thinking.0: Comparing values on different scales against the same standard
y-m-78-03.thinking.1: Finding the line in the working where the comparison standard is misused
y-m-78-03.thinking.2: Stating the conditions under which the comparison holds
y-m-78-03.prereq.0: This task is at the 'H1' difficulty (introductory high school level) in this platform's production allocation, and it does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this subject to a particular grade. Assume you already know the prerequisite concepts below.
y-m-78-03.prereq.1: The meaning of mean and standard deviation (how spread out the data is around the mean)
y-m-78-03.prereq.2: Calculating the difference between a score and the mean
y-m-78-03.s.s1.prompt: Hayun says, 'I'm 18 points above the mean in math, so math is the subject I did relatively better in.' When comparing position within the grade, what is the most fitting judgment?
y-m-78-03.s.s1.hint.0: For each subject, find how many times the standard deviation the difference from the mean is, and compare.
y-m-78-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how how spread out the scores are around the mean changes the meaning of the same 12 points and 18 points.
y-m-78-03.s.s1.o.a: Korean (82), where the score itself is higher, is the subject done relatively better.
y-m-78-03.s.s1.r.a: What a high score means depends on whether the test was easy or hard. You need to look at the value compared with the grade mean.
y-m-78-03.s.s1.o.b: Math (18 points), where the difference from the mean is larger, is the subject done better.
y-m-78-03.s.s1.r.b: You compared the differences in scores as they are. In math the scores are more spread out, so 18 points means something different from Korean's 12 points.
y-m-78-03.s.s1.o.c: Using the size of the standard deviation as the unit and looking at how many of them away from the mean, Korean is in a higher position.
y-m-78-03.s.s1.r.c: You changed to a distance measured by how spread out the data is and compared. You made the units of the scores the same and then compared.
y-m-78-03.s.s1.o.d: We don't know the test difficulty or the shape of the score distribution, so we can't judge which is in a higher position.
y-m-78-03.s.s1.r.d: This is a careful attitude of wanting to confirm the shape of the distribution. However, since the mean and standard deviation are given, you can first look at whether there is a comparison you can make with them.
y-m-78-03.s.s1.explain: In Korean, the score is 12 points above the mean and the standard deviation is 6, so it is 2 standard deviations above the mean. In math, it is 18 points above with a standard deviation of 12, so 1.5 standard deviations above. So within the grade, Korean is in the higher position. It is also reasonable to hold off judging while not knowing even the shape of the distribution.
y-m-78-03.s.s1.acc.0: A careful judgment not to settle on a position without knowing the shape of the distribution and the nature of the test is also valid. However, you should confirm that there is information you can compare with just the mean and standard deviation.
y-m-78-03.s.s2.prompt: This is a write-up by a student organizing the comparison above. Choose one line in which the comparison standard is misused.
y-m-78-03.s.s2.hint.0: For each line, check separately whether the numbers are right and whether the 'reason' for using those numbers is right.
y-m-78-03.s.s2.hint.1: The standard deviation was found in line 4, so look at whether it is used in the lines after that.
y-m-78-03.s.s2.line.0: Korean: 82−70=12 points, so it is 12 points above the mean.
y-m-78-03.s.s2.line.1: Math: 74−56=18 points, so it is 18 points above the mean.
y-m-78-03.s.s2.line.2: 18 points is greater than 12 points, so math is in a relatively higher position.
y-m-78-03.s.s2.line.3: The standard deviation of Korean is 6, and the standard deviation of math is 12.
y-m-78-03.s.s2.line.4: Even if the spread differs from test to test, comparing the differences in scores directly is the fairest.
y-m-78-03.s.s2.explain: Lines 3 and 5 are the problem. The spread of scores differs from test to test, so you must not compare 12 points and 18 points as they are. You need to compare the values divided by the standard deviation found in line 4 (Korean 2, math 1.5).
y-m-78-03.s.s3.prompt: You are going to tell Hayun that 'Korean is in a relatively higher position'. For this comparison to be trustworthy, write in one or two sentences what needs to be similar in the two tests, or what needs to be checked further.
y-m-78-03.s.s3.hint.0: Turn each subject's 'difference from the mean' into 'how many times the standard deviation'.
y-m-78-03.s.s3.hint.1: Write down what you assumed to be the same in the two tests when comparing those values.
y-m-78-03.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If we compare using the standard deviation, ...
y-m-78-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is the evidence I wrote 'a value that takes the spread into account' rather than 'the difference in scores'?
y-m-78-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write specifically at least one condition needed for the comparison to be trustworthy?
y-m-78-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I stay within the scope 'a higher position within the grade' rather than saying 'did better in Korean'?
y-m-78-03.s.s3.model.0: Korean is 2 standard deviations above the mean and math is 1.5, so Korean is in a higher position. However, this comparison is more trustworthy if the score distributions of the two tests are roughly symmetric and bell-shaped, and the tests were taken by the same grade.
y-m-78-03.s.s3.model.1: When divided by the standard deviation, Korean is 2 and math is 1.5, so Korean is ahead. But if the math test was very hard and the scores were bunched on the low side, the distribution may not be symmetric, so I want to check the shape of the score distributions of the two subjects further.
y-m-78-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that says it will check the shape of the distribution is also valid.

y-m-78-04.title: Does the 'most common range' depend on how you make the table?
y-m-78-04.topic: Setting classes and interpreting a frequency distribution table
y-m-78-04.goal: Know that changing the starting point and the width of the classes can make a frequency distribution table look different, find the error in a sentence that reads a table, and rewrite it so readers are not misled.
y-m-78-04.material:
A survey recorded the average daily sleep time (hours) of 30 students at one school (recorded in steps of 0.5 hours). The same data was shown in three tables with the classes set differently. In the tables, 'at least ~ less than' means the first value is included and the last value is not.

**Table A (starting at 5 hours, width 1 hour)**
| Class (hours) | 5~6 | 6~7 | 7~8 | 8~9 | 9~10 | 10~11 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Number of students | 3 | 7 | 13 | 5 | 1 | 1 |

**Table B (starting at 5.5 hours, width 1 hour)**
| Class (hours) | 5.5~6.5 | 6.5~7.5 | 7.5~8.5 | 8.5~9.5 | 9.5~10.5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Number of students | 7 | 12 | 8 | 2 | 1 |

**Table C (starting at 4 hours, width 2 hours)**
| Class (hours) | 4~6 | 6~8 | 8~10 | 10~12 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Number of students | 3 | 20 | 6 | 1 |
y-m-78-04.thinking.0: Comparing the results of showing the same data in different tables
y-m-78-04.thinking.1: Finding and fixing errors in sentences that interpret a table
y-m-78-04.thinking.2: Pointing out how the way of presenting affects interpretation
y-m-78-04.prereq.0: This task is at the 'H1' difficulty (introductory high school level) in this platform's production allocation, and it does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this subject to a particular grade. Assume you already know the prerequisite concepts below.
y-m-78-04.prereq.1: The meaning of class, frequency, and relative frequency in a frequency distribution table
y-m-78-04.prereq.2: The convention that classes are divided as 'at least ~ less than'
y-m-78-04.s.s1.prompt: A reporter wrote this after looking at the three tables. Choose one line in which the interpretation of a table is wrong.
y-m-78-04.s.s1.hint.0: For each of Tables A and B, add up all the frequencies and check whether they match the total number of students.
y-m-78-04.s.s1.hint.1: Change the 20 students in line 5 yourself into a ratio of the total of 30.
y-m-78-04.s.s1.line.0: In Table A, the class with the most students is 7 hours or more and less than 8 hours (13 students).
y-m-78-04.s.s1.line.1: In Table B, the class with the most students is 6.5 hours or more and less than 7.5 hours (12 students).
y-m-78-04.s.s1.line.2: The classes with the most students differ between the two tables, so one of the two was made incorrectly.
y-m-78-04.s.s1.line.3: Even though the width and starting point of the classes differ, both tables are the same in that students are concentrated around 7 hours.
y-m-78-04.s.s1.line.4: In Table C, the number of students from 6 hours up to less than 8 hours is 20, which is 20% of the total.
y-m-78-04.s.s1.explain: Lines 3 and 5 are the problem. Line 3: the classes were simply set differently, and both tables are tables that count the same data correctly. Line 5: 20 students is about 67% of the total of 30 (20% is the ratio when it would be about 6 students, not 20).
y-m-78-04.s.s2.prompt: The class with the most students turned out differently in Table A and Table B. Based on this fact, what is the most fitting response?
y-m-78-04.s.s2.hint.0: For each of Tables A, B, and C, write in one line the time range where the most students gather.
y-m-78-04.s.s2.hint.1: Separate what the three tables say in common from what they say differently.
y-m-78-04.s.s2.o.a: Try changing the classes, and take only the features that do not change as the conclusion.
y-m-78-04.s.s2.r.a: You separated what stays the same and what changes when the table settings change.
y-m-78-04.s.s2.o.b: Table A was made first, so trust only Table A's result and ignore Table B and Table C.
y-m-78-04.s.s2.r.b: The order they were made in has nothing to do with how far to trust the result.
y-m-78-04.s.s2.o.c: The classes with the most are different in the two tables, so the data must have been counted wrong.
y-m-78-04.s.s2.r.c: The data is the same and only the classes differ. The tables looking different is not because the data is wrong.
y-m-78-04.s.s2.o.d: Strongly emphasize only the single class with the largest frequency and use it as an article headline.
y-m-78-04.s.s2.r.d: If you emphasize only one class, you end up taking even the part that changes with the table settings as the conclusion.
y-m-78-04.s.s2.explain: Depending on the starting point and width of the classes, the class with the most can change. It is not that one of the tables is wrong; the window you look through is different. It is safer to take as the conclusion the features that hold across several settings.
y-m-78-04.s.s3.prompt: Looking only at Table A, you are going to write in an article that 'the most students sleep in the 7-hour range (7 hours or more and less than 8 hours)'. Write how you would fix or add to the sentence so readers are not misled.
y-m-78-04.s.s3.hint.0: Write down what readers of the article do not know.
y-m-78-04.s.s3.hint.1: Check how the class with the most turned out in Table B, and reflect it in the sentence.
y-m-78-04.s.s3.placeholder: Example: This table is divided in the way of ...
y-m-78-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the fixed sentence avoid the definite claim 'exactly the 7-hour range'?
y-m-78-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you let readers know how the classes were divided?
y-m-78-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you add a feature that holds in the other tables too?
y-m-78-04.s.s3.model.0: This table shows the result of dividing in steps of 1 hour starting from 5 hours. Even when divided differently, it appears similarly that the most students are gathered around 7 hours.
y-m-78-04.s.s3.model.1: The most students (13) are in the class of 7 hours or more and less than 8 hours, but in another table with the classes divided starting at 5.5 hours, 6.5 hours or more and less than 7.5 hours (12 students) has the most, so you should add that it is hard to claim it is exactly the 7-hour range.

y-m-78-05.title: Daily sales went down: is the business going downhill?
y-m-78-05.topic: Reading a time series with day-of-week effects: comparing the same weekdays and 7-day averages
y-m-78-05.goal: In data with a repeating pattern, do not settle on a trend from a one-day difference alone, look at the change by comparing the same weekdays or using 7-day averages, and evaluate how new information affects judging the cause.
y-m-78-05.material: The owner of a neighborhood bakery records the number sold each day by day of the week. This week's Sunday sales came out lower than last Saturday's, and the owner is worried. The data is values recorded at the same time every day at this bakery, and only days of similar scale (excluding public holidays) were collected.
y-m-78-05.thinking.0: Revising your judgment and confidence as the data grows
y-m-78-05.thinking.1: Choosing a comparison method that takes the repeating pattern into account
y-m-78-05.thinking.2: Separating what a candidate cause explains from what it does not explain
y-m-78-05.prereq.0: This task is at the 'H1' difficulty (introductory high school level) in this platform's production allocation, and it does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this subject to a particular grade. Assume you already know the prerequisite concepts below.
y-m-78-05.prereq.2: How to compare values in the same position in a table
y-m-78-05.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed in steps. Each time, choose the most fitting thought with the information so far.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.hint.0: Pair up the same weekdays, write them in a table, and find the differences.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.hint.1: Write separately the days that the new information explains (weekdays) and the days it does not explain (weekend).
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.0.info: Number sold in week 1 (Mon to Sun): 120, 118, 125, 122, 160, 210, 205. Sunday (205) is 5 fewer than Saturday (210).
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.0.ask: The owner worries that 'sales have started to fall'. With the data so far, what is the most fitting judgment?
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.0.after: A change between two days is mixed with the weekday pattern, so it is hard to tell whether sales are falling. Comparing the same weekdays or comparing 7-day totals (averages) reduces the effect of the pattern.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It dropped by 5 from Saturday, so I think sales have started to fall.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You settled on a trend from a change between two days alone. Weekends and weekdays may be very different to begin with.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Weekdays and weekends are very different to begin with, so it is hard to judge from a one-day difference.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You found the repeating pattern that the sales level differs by day of the week.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.0.o.c: On weekends sales are similar every day, so the difference of 5 has no meaning at all.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Friday to Sunday are also different from each other at 160, 210, and 205. It is too early to say 'no meaning at all'.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Monday to Thursday are almost the same, so this shop's sales are constant.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You looked only at weekdays and said the whole is constant. The weekend values are very different from weekdays.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.1.info: Number sold in week 2 (Mon to Sun): 108, 106, 112, 110, 150, 198, 190. The 7-day total is 1060 for week 1 (about 151.4 per day on average) and 974 for week 2 (about 139.1 per day).
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.1.after: That all 7 days fell in the same direction is a meaningful clue. However, since there are only two weeks, we can't know whether it will continue.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Comparing the same weekdays, all 7 days fell, so there is now evidence that it fell.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You paired the same weekdays instead of single days, and used as evidence that every weekday moved in the same direction.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Week 2's Friday (150) is more than Monday (108), so sales are growing.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You compared values from different weekdays. Friday being more than Monday is the weekday pattern.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.1.o.c: All 7 days fell, but there are only two weeks, so we can't know whether it will continue.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You pointed out that the fact that it fell and whether it will continue are separate.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.1.o.d: The total fell, so we can conclude that this bakery is steadily going downhill.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You concluded even the future trend from the change over two weeks.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.2.info: New information: during the 5 days Monday to Friday of week 2, the road in front of the bakery was blocked by construction and customers dropped. On Saturday and Sunday the road was open. The decrease by day was Mon 12, Tue 12, Wed 13, Thu 12, Fri 10, Sat 12, Sun 15.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.2.ask: After learning this, how is it fitting to judge?
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.2.after: The road construction can explain part of the weekday decrease, but since sales also fell on the weekend, when there was no construction, there may be another cause. Before settling that there is one cause, you should compare next week's data with the same weekdays.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It fell because of the construction, so it's temporary and there's no need to worry.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The road was open on Saturday and Sunday, yet sales fell by 12 and 15. There is a part that the construction alone does not explain.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It fell regardless of the construction, so the shop's popularity has clearly dropped.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Part of the weekday decrease may be due to the construction. There is also not yet any ground to settle that the cause is a drop in popularity.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The weekday decrease may be due to the construction, but the weekend also fell, so keep watching.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You separated the part the construction explains from the part it does not.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The decrease by day is similar on weekdays and weekends, so the construction had no effect at all.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You can't conclude the construction had no effect just because the weekday decrease (about 10 to 13) and the weekend decrease (12 to 15) are similar.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.reflect: Was your first judgment unchanged, or how did it change as the data grew? Tell how your confidence changed for each of: a one-day difference, same-weekday comparison, and the candidate cause.
y-m-78-05.s.s2.prompt: The owner says they will compare the '7-day average' every week from now on. Write in one or two sentences what gets better with the 7-day average, and what in exchange becomes harder to see.
y-m-78-05.s.s2.hint.0: Compare whether the difference between week 1's and week 2's 7-day averages is similar to the differences by weekday.
y-m-78-05.s.s2.hint.1: Think of one thing that cannot be seen in a 7-day average.
y-m-78-05.s.s2.placeholder: Example: If you use a 7-day average, ...
y-m-78-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write specifically how the 7-day average reduces the ups and downs by day of the week?
y-m-78-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you give an example of what the 7-day average hides (for example, a case where only one weekday fell)?
y-m-78-05.s.s2.model.0: When you average 7 days, weekdays and weekends are mixed, so the fluctuations that repeat by weekday shrink and it becomes easier to compare the week-to-week trend. In exchange, which day of the week had the change, and anything that suddenly changed in a single day, is hidden by the average.
y-m-78-05.s.s2.model.1: Using a weekly average lets you see the trend without being swayed by the weekday pattern. However, you can miss details such as only Friday falling a lot within a week, so you should look at the table by weekday as well.
y-m-78-05.s.s2.modelNote.1: The suggestion to use the by-weekday comparison together is valid.

y-m-78-06.title: What does an index of 126 mean?
y-m-78-06.topic: Index and growth rate: reading values relative to a base year
y-m-78-06.goal: In an index with the base year set to 100, tell apart the change (points) and the growth rate (%), make an example yourself where the two come out differently, and sort out what cannot be known from the index alone.
y-m-78-06.material:
A price index sets the price of the base year (2020) to 100 and expresses the prices of other years. The index of one item is as follows.

| Year | 2020 | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Index | 100 | 105 | 115 | 126 |

(The 2020 price is the base, so the index is 100.)
y-m-78-06.thinking.0: Checking whether the units (%, %p) and the base match in the working lines
y-m-78-06.thinking.1: Making a counterexample that satisfies the conditions yourself
y-m-78-06.thinking.2: Sorting out information that cannot be known from the index alone
y-m-78-06.prereq.0: This task is at the 'H1' difficulty (introductory high school level) in this platform's production allocation, and it does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this subject to a particular grade. Assume you already know the prerequisite concepts below.
y-m-78-06.prereq.1: The meaning of percentages and ratios
y-m-78-06.prereq.2: Calculating the ratio of a change to some value
y-m-78-06.s.s1.prompt: This is the working a student wrote after reading the index table. Choose one line whose content is wrong.
y-m-78-06.s.s1.hint.0: Think about what the 2023 index would be if you treated the 2021 index of 105 as the 'new 100'.
y-m-78-06.s.s1.hint.1: Compare how the base differs between lines like 1 and 5, where the base is 2020, and line 3.
y-m-78-06.s.s1.line.0: The 2023 index of 126 means that the price rose 26% above the base year (2020).
y-m-78-06.s.s1.line.1: The 2021 index of 105 means that the price rose 5% above the base year.
y-m-78-06.s.s1.line.3: Therefore, if an item that cost 1,000원 in 2021 rose by the same rate, it is 1,210원 in 2023.
y-m-78-06.s.s1.line.4: If an item that cost 1,000원 in 2020 rose by the same rate, it is 1,260원 in 2023.
y-m-78-06.s.s1.explain: Lines 3 and 4 are the problem. Line 3: 126−105=21 means the index rose by 21 points, and the growth rate based on the 2021 price (105) is 126÷105=1.2, that is, 20%. Line 4: if it rose 20%, 1,000원 becomes 1,200원.
y-m-78-06.s.s2.prompt:
Decide the 2021 and 2023 indexes of two items A and B. (All are indexes where 2020 is 100.) Enter 2 different examples that satisfy all of the following conditions.
① All indexes are integers from 50 to 200
② For both items, the 2023 index is greater than the 2021 index
③ A's change in index (points) is smaller than B's
④ The growth rate compared with 2021 is greater for A than for B
y-m-78-06.s.s2.hint.0: Try setting A's 2021 index small and B's 2021 index large, and first compare the changes (points) of the two items.
y-m-78-06.s.s2.hint.1: For each set of values, calculate the ratio of 2023 to 2021 and check whether ④ holds.
y-m-78-06.s.s2.ok.c1: All indexes are integers from 50 to 200.
y-m-78-06.s.s2.fail.c1: The indexes must be integers from 50 to 200.
y-m-78-06.s.s2.ok.c2: For both items, the 2023 index is greater.
y-m-78-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The 2023 index must be greater than the 2021 index.
y-m-78-06.s.s2.ok.c3: A's change (points) is smaller than B's.
y-m-78-06.s.s2.fail.c3: A's change in index is not smaller than B's change.
y-m-78-06.s.s2.ok.c4: A's growth rate is greater than B's.
y-m-78-06.s.s2.fail.c4: A's growth rate (2023 index ÷ 2021 index) is not greater than B's.
y-m-78-06.s.s2.explain: For example, if A goes from 100 to 115, up 15 points (15%), and B goes from 160 to 180, up 20 points (12.5%), A's points are smaller but A's growth rate is greater. For an item whose 2021 index is small, even the same change in points looks larger as a ratio.
y-m-78-06.s.s3.prompt: A student said, 'Item A's 2023 index is 130 and item B's is 110, so item A is more expensive than item B.' What is the most fitting judgment about this statement?
y-m-78-06.s.s3.hint.0: Try putting in a number for each item, assuming what its base-year price is, and see what happens.
y-m-78-06.s.s3.hint.1: Tell apart whether what the index 130 points to is the price itself or a ratio to the base price.
y-m-78-06.s.s3.o.a: The index is higher at 130, so item A's price is higher than item B's.
y-m-78-06.s.s3.r.a: The index is a value with each item's own base-year price as 100. It is not a value that lets you compare the prices of different items directly.
y-m-78-06.s.s3.o.b: The index is a value relative to each item's own base year, so the actual price can't be known.
y-m-78-06.s.s3.r.b: You pointed out that each index has a different base.
y-m-78-06.s.s3.o.c: Item A's change (points) is always larger than item B's in 2023.
y-m-78-06.s.s3.r.c: 130 and 110 are just indexes for the same year. It doesn't say which year the change is measured from.
y-m-78-06.s.s3.o.d: The difference of 20 in the two items' indexes means the price difference is 20원.
y-m-78-06.s.s3.r.d: A difference in indexes is not a difference in price (원). The units are different.
y-m-78-06.s.s3.explain: The index is a value 'when the base-year price is taken as 100', so it is good for comparing changes over time of the same item. To tell which of different items is higher or lower, or their actual prices, you need to know more about the base-year prices.

y-m-78-07.title: A is ahead in the total, but B is ahead class by class?
y-m-78-07.topic: When the conclusion flips after splitting into groups (mixing effect)
y-m-78-07.goal: Confirm that the overall ratio and the group ratios can go in different directions, make such numbers yourself, and explain why you should not conclude cause from data the students chose for themselves.
y-m-78-07.material: A survey asked 100 students each who used English vocabulary learning apps A and B for one semester whether they exceeded the target score (70 points) on the end-of-semester vocabulary test. The students are 'advanced class' and 'basic class' students at one school. The two apps are said to have the same price and the same usage time.
y-m-78-07.thinking.0: Revising your judgment when you look at the data split into parts
y-m-78-07.thinking.1: Making numbers that give ratios in opposite directions yourself
y-m-78-07.thinking.2: Evaluating how the way the data was gathered affects the conclusion
y-m-78-07.prereq.0: This task is at the 'H2' difficulty (one step beyond H1) in this platform's production allocation, and it does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this subject to a particular grade. Assume you already know the prerequisite concepts below.
y-m-78-07.prereq.1: How to compare ratios (number of students who passed ÷ total number of students)
y-m-78-07.prereq.2: Reading a table that splits the whole data into groups
y-m-78-07.prereq.3: H1-level concepts of sample and representative value
y-m-78-07.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed in steps. Each time, choose the most fitting judgment with the information so far.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.hint.0: Write the pass rate of each class and the number of students in each class side by side.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.hint.1: Count which class the 100 students who used app A came from.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.0.info: Overall results: of the 100 students who used app A, 78 exceeded the target score, and of the 100 students who used app B, 47 did.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is the most fitting judgment now?
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.0.after: The difference in pass rates is a fact, but we can't tell whether this difference is because of the app. First look at whether the two groups are similar.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.0.o.a: A has a higher pass rate than B, so A is a much more effective app.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You went straight from the fact that the pass rates differ to the conclusion that the effects differ. We don't yet know whether the students who used the two apps are similar groups.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.0.o.b: A has the higher pass rate, but we don't know whether the two groups are similar, so it is too early to settle the effect.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You separated the observed difference from its cause.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.0.o.c: With 100 students each, that is a large number, so this difference can't be chance and is due to the app.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Even with many people, if the two groups were different from the start, it may not be because of the app.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.0.o.d: There is only one ratio, so it gives no information for comparing the two apps.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.0.r.d: The pass rates being different is clear information. You just need to be careful in how you state what that information means.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.1.info:
These are the results split by class.
Advanced class: app A 72 of 80 students (90%), app B 19 of 20 students (95%).
Basic class: app A 6 of 20 students (30%), app B 28 of 80 students (35%).
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.1.ask: A was higher in the total, but class by class it looks different. What do you think?
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.1.after: The advanced class has a high pass rate to begin with. 80 of the 100 students who used A were in the advanced class, which raised the total. Comparing within the same class, B is slightly higher.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.1.o.a: A was higher in the total, so we disregard the class results and say A is better.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.1.r.a: The overall ratio may be high because most of the students who used A were in the class where passing is easier.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.1.o.b: B's pass rate is higher in both classes, so we conclude B is more effective without considering other factors.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Comparing by class is better than the total, but differences among the students who used the apps may remain even within a class.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Within the same class B is slightly higher, and A's total may be high because advanced students were concentrated in it.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You found that a difference in group makeup can change the total.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.1.o.d: The results differ from class to class, so we can't tell at all which app is better.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.1.r.d: B is slightly higher in both classes, the same direction. The results are not conflicting.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.2.info: The students chose the app themselves. Of the 100 students in the advanced class, 80 chose A, and of the 100 students in the basic class, 80 chose B. The reasons for their choices were not surveyed.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.2.ask: After learning this, how is it fitting to conclude?
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.2.after: Split by class, B is slightly higher, but the way the students chose the apps can affect passing. To know the effect of an app, you need a different design, such as dividing students randomly to use each one.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.2.o.a: B was higher when comparing within the same class, so we conclude B is effective regardless of how they chose.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Even within the same class, the students chose by themselves, so students with different motivation or ability may have ended up in different groups.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The difference between the two apps is small, so we conclude the effects are completely the same.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.2.r.b: A small difference is not evidence that they are the same.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Data the students chose by themselves can't be trusted, so throw it all out and start over.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The data holds information. You need to write distinguishing which questions it can answer.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.2.o.d: B is slightly higher class by class, but since it is self-chosen data, other factors remain, so we do not settle on the effect.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You separated the observed difference from the effect of the app, and pointed out the uncertainty left by the selection process.
y-m-78-07.s.s1.reflect: How did your confidence differ when you looked at the total only, when you split by class, and when you learned that the students chose by themselves? At which step did you revise your judgment, and which judgment did you not revise?
y-m-78-07.s.s2.prompt:
Make an example yourself with other apps C and D in which the total and the class results go in opposite directions. y-m-78-07.s.s2.var.d1: Number who passed for D in the advanced class (out of 10)

y-m-78-08.title: What does a correlation coefficient of -0.6 tell us, and what does it not tell us?
y-m-78-08.topic: The meaning and limits of the correlation coefficient
y-m-78-08.goal: Know that the correlation coefficient shows only the direction and strength of a straight-line relationship and does not mean the slope or a cause, and make an example yourself where the coefficient is near 0 but there is a clear relationship.
y-m-78-08.material: The correlation coefficient between the daily smartphone use time (hours) and sleep time (hours) of 20 students came out to be −0.6. The scatter plot shows the points spread in a band that generally slopes down to the lower right. The correlation coefficient is a number from −1 to 1 that shows the direction and strength of the straight-line relationship between two variables (0 means no straight-line relationship is seen).
y-m-78-08.thinking.0: Finding errors in sentences that interpret a correlation coefficient
y-m-78-08.thinking.1: Sorting out cases where there is a relationship even though the coefficient is 0
y-m-78-08.thinking.2: Making a counterexample that satisfies the conditions
y-m-78-08.prereq.0: This task is at the 'H2' difficulty (one step beyond H1) in this platform's production allocation, and it does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this subject to a particular grade. Assume you already know the prerequisite concepts below.
y-m-78-08.prereq.1: How to read the relationship of two variables (positive correlation, negative correlation) from a scatter plot
y-m-78-08.prereq.2: The idea that the correlation coefficient is between -1 and 1 and shows the strength of a straight-line relationship
y-m-78-08.prereq.3: Reading a table and putting values into a formula
y-m-78-08.s.s1.prompt: A student wrote an interpretation of the correlation coefficient −0.6. Choose one wrong line.
y-m-78-08.s.s1.hint.0: First sort each line by whether it speaks about the direction, strength, slope, or cause of the correlation.
y-m-78-08.s.s1.hint.1: Imagine what happens when you apply line 5 to a scatter plot whose points are placed in a U shape.
y-m-78-08.s.s1.line.0: It means that the longer the use time, the shorter the sleep time tends to be.
y-m-78-08.s.s1.line.1: Therefore, for every 1 hour the use time increases, the sleep time decreases by 0.6 hours.
y-m-78-08.s.s1.line.2: How far the relationship between the two variables departs from a straight line is reflected in the size of the correlation coefficient.
y-m-78-08.s.s1.line.3: From this data alone, it is hard to say for sure that the smartphone caused the sleep to shrink.
y-m-78-08.s.s1.line.4: If the correlation coefficient were 0, there would be no relationship of any kind between the two variables.
y-m-78-08.s.s1.explain: Lines 2 and 5 are the problem. Line 2: the correlation coefficient is the direction and strength of the relationship, not the slope. How many hours it drops when it rises by 1 hour has to be found with a separate line (the regression line). Line 5: a correlation coefficient of 0 means 'there is no straight-line relationship', and there can be other relationships, such as a curved one.
y-m-78-08.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the scatter plots where the correlation coefficient is near 0 but there is a clear relationship between the two variables. (The scatter plots are described in words.)
y-m-78-08.s.s2.hint.0: For each shape, look at whether y moves overall in only one direction as x gets larger.
y-m-78-08.s.s2.hint.1: Split x into a left half and a right half and compare the trend of each.
y-m-78-08.s.s2.o.a: The points form a straight band from the lower left to the upper right.
y-m-78-08.s.s2.r.a: A shape close to a straight band has a correlation coefficient whose absolute value is close to 1.
y-m-78-08.s.s2.o.b: The points are placed in a symmetric U shape.
y-m-78-08.s.s2.r.b: For a curve that is symmetric left and right, the trends in each direction cancel each other, so the correlation coefficient can be near 0.
y-m-78-08.s.s2.o.c: The points are scattered with no particular shape.
y-m-78-08.s.s2.r.c: The correlation coefficient is near 0 because there is no relationship. But this is not a case with a clear relationship.
y-m-78-08.s.s2.o.d: The points are placed in a ring (round band) shape.
y-m-78-08.s.s2.r.d: In a ring shape, even when x is fixed, y splits into two values, so the correlation coefficient can be near 0.
y-m-78-08.s.s2.explain: The correlation coefficient measures only straight-line relationships. A relationship that has a clear rule but is not a straight line, like a U shape, has a relationship even if the coefficient is near 0. The case where the points are just scattered (c) is a case with no relationship.
y-m-78-08.s.s3.prompt:
Let x be −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, and decide y using the following conditions. This is data of 5 points. Enter 2 different examples where the correlation coefficient is 0 and y is determined from x by a clear rule. (y1, y2, y3, y4, y5 are the y values when x is −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, integers)
① y is symmetric left and right about x=0 (y1=y5, y2=y4)
② y1, y2, y3 keep increasing or keep decreasing (U shape or ∩ shape)
y-m-78-08.s.s3.hint.0: Check what the sum of products becomes when you set y equal for x=−2 and x=2.
y-m-78-08.s.s3.hint.1: Decide the numbers one by one so that y1, y2, y3 keep decreasing (for example, from a large value to a small value).
y-m-78-08.s.s3.ok.c1: It is symmetric left and right.
y-m-78-08.s.s3.fail.c1: It is not the case that y1=y5 and y2=y4.
y-m-78-08.s.s3.ok.c2: y1, y2, y3 keep increasing or keep decreasing.
y-m-78-08.s.s3.fail.c2: y1, y2, y3 do not change in only one direction.
y-m-78-08.s.s3.ok.c4: The sum of the products of x and y is 0, so the correlation coefficient is 0.
y-m-78-08.s.s3.fail.c4: It does not satisfy the condition for the correlation coefficient to be 0.
y-m-78-08.s.s3.explain: The mean of x is 0, so if the sum of the products of x and y is 0, the correlation coefficient is 0. Points that are symmetric left and right have a sum of products of 0. For example, the values of y=x² (4, 1, 0, 1, 4) have x completely determining y, but the correlation coefficient is 0.

y-m-78-09.title: If I put 38 degrees into the line's equation I get 214, so can I prepare that many?
y-m-78-09.topic: The range and limits of predicting with a regression line
y-m-78-09.goal: Know that a regression line is a usable approximation within the range where the data was collected, decide how to adjust your judgment about predictions outside the range and in front of new data, and write usage instructions.
y-m-78-09.material: An ice cream shop recorded the daily highest temperature x (°C) and the number sold y over the last 20 days. The highest temperature on every day was between 20°C and 30°C. The scatter plot shows the points in a band rising to the upper right, and the correlation coefficient is 0.93. The least-squares regression line found from this data is ŷ=8x−90 (read as 'y hat equals 8 times x minus 90').
y-m-78-09.thinking.0: Recognizing the uncertainty of predicted values
y-m-78-09.thinking.1: Judging the risk of predictions outside the range of the data
y-m-78-09.thinking.2: Revising the range where the model applies with new data
y-m-78-09.prereq.0: This task is at the 'H2' difficulty (one step beyond H1) in this platform's production allocation, and it does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this subject to a particular grade. Assume you already know the prerequisite concepts below.
y-m-78-09.prereq.1: Scatter plots and calculating by putting values into the line's equation y=ax+b
y-m-78-09.prereq.2: The meaning of the correlation coefficient (direction and strength of a relationship)
y-m-78-09.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed in steps. Each time, choose the most fitting judgment with the information so far.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.hint.0: Write the range of temperatures used to find the line, and compare whether the temperature you want to predict is inside or outside it.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the predicted value made by putting a value into the line is a possible actual value (a count that is not negative).
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.0.info: Tomorrow's forecast highest temperature is 25°C. Putting 25 into the line gives ŷ=110.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is the most fitting judgment about tomorrow's sales?
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.0.after: 25°C is inside the observed range (20 to 30°C), so the predicted 110 is a usable reference. The actual value can differ because the points are scattered.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It is the value of putting 25 into the line, so exactly 110 will be sold tomorrow.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.0.r.a: The points are scattered around the line, so actual sales can differ from the line's value.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.0.o.b: The correlation coefficient is 0.93, so about 102, which is 110 multiplied by 0.93, will be sold.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.0.r.b: The correlation coefficient is not a number that you multiply the predicted value by.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Sales can differ even at the same temperature, so I think of it as around 110.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You took into account that sales scatter even at the same temperature and used the predicted value as a rough reference.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Even with the line, tomorrow's sales can't be known at all.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.0.r.d: The line summarizes the tendency of how temperature affects sales. 25°C is inside the range of the data, so it is a usable reference.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.1.info: The forecast for next week says a heat wave will bring a highest temperature of 38°C. Putting 38 into the line gives ŷ=214.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.1.ask: How is it fitting to treat this 214?
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.1.after: 38°C is outside the observed range. The 214 is a value that assumes the line continues, so use it only as a reference, and the careful attitude of not stating any number is also reasonable.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Sales at 25°C were 110, so I think about 165, 1.5 times that, will be sold.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.1.r.a: The line's equation is y=8x−90, so if the temperature becomes 1.5 times, sales do not become 1.5 times. Putting in 38 gives 214, and this method does not fit.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 214 came out, so I believe it as is and prepare the ingredients.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.1.r.b: 38°C is a range that was not in the data. We have never checked whether the line continues into that range.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It's outside the range, so it's a value that assumes the line continues; use it only as a reference.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You noticed the assumption that the line will continue and lowered your trust in the predicted value.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It's outside the observed range, so no number can be given for sales.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Using no number at all may be overly careful. It is more useful to state the assumption and use it as a reference value.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.2.info: The shop also opened on a day with a temperature of 12°C and sold 25. Putting 12 into the line gives ŷ=6. If the temperature is 11°C or lower, the line's value becomes negative.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is the most fitting thing this new data tells us?
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.2.after: If you widen the temperature range, the shape of the relationship may not be a straight line. The line is a usable approximation within the range observed, so to widen the range you have to check it again with data from that range.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The data at 12°C is a strange value that departs greatly from the line, so it should be removed from the analysis.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Before throwing out data, you should look for the reason it differs from the line. This value tells us the limit of the line.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The line also fits well at low temperatures outside 20 to 30°C as it is.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.2.r.b: At 12°C the line's value is 6, but the actual is 25. It doesn't fit well at low temperatures.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Sales have no relationship with temperature, and they just happened to rise so far.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.2.r.c: In 20 to 30°C there was a clear relationship. If you widen the range, only the shape of the relationship changes.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The line may be usable only in 20 to 30°C, so check it again if you widen the range.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You found that the range of the data decides the range where the model applies.
y-m-78-09.s.s1.reflect: How did you first take the line's value, and how did it change when you met the prediction outside the range and the new data? Why did your degree of trust change even though it is the same line?
y-m-78-09.s.s2.prompt: The shop owner wants to use this line every day. Write a note of two or three sentences for the owner on what to watch out for when using this line.
y-m-78-09.s.s2.hint.0: Write in one sentence the range of highest temperatures in the data used to make the line.
y-m-78-09.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what to do to use the line safely outside the range.
y-m-78-09.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you state the temperature range where the line can be used with specific numbers?
y-m-78-09.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you suggest what to do outside the range (use only as a reference, check again)?
y-m-78-09.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you mention that sales can differ even at the same temperature?
y-m-78-09.s.s2.model.0: Please use this line as a reference only when the temperature is 20 to 30°C. For other temperatures the line may not fit, so use it only as a reference. Even at the same temperature, actual sales can differ from the line's value.
y-m-78-09.s.s2.model.1: The line was made with data between 20°C and 30°C, so it is usable within that range, but if you go outside the range, like 38°C, it is hard to be sure even if 214 comes out, so use it only as a reference. In a new temperature range, collect data and check the line again.

y-m-78-10.title: 52% in favor, margin of error ±3.1%p: can we write that it's a majority?
y-m-78-10.topic: Reading a confidence interval: can we say it is a majority?
y-m-78-10.goal: Decide how strong a conclusion is by whether the confidence interval includes the reference value (50%), explain in words how the judgment changes when the sample gets larger, and explain the meaning of 95%.
y-m-78-10.material: A city surveyed for and against 'building a new library'. Of 1,000 randomly chosen citizens, 52% were in favor, and the 95% confidence interval was calculated as about 48.9% to 55.1% (margin of error ±3.1%p). A reporter wants to use the headline 'Majority of citizens in favor'. The survey was done by phone, and assume the response rate was not low.
y-m-78-10.thinking.0: Judging by comparing the confidence interval with the reference value
y-m-78-10.thinking.1: Evaluating how new data affects the judgment
y-m-78-10.prereq.0: This task is at the 'H2' difficulty (one step beyond H1) in this platform's production allocation, and it does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this subject to a particular grade. Assume you already know the prerequisite concepts below.
y-m-78-10.prereq.1: The difference between a sample proportion and a population proportion, and why the proportion differs from sample to sample
y-m-78-10.prereq.2: How to read a margin of error written with '±' as an interval (smaller value to larger value)
y-m-78-10.prereq.3: A rough idea of what value a 95% confidence interval is trying to express
y-m-78-10.s.s1.prompt: What is the most fitting judgment about the reporter's headline 'Majority of citizens in favor'?
y-m-78-10.s.s1.hint.0: Compare the lower end and the upper end of the confidence interval with 50%.
y-m-78-10.s.s1.hint.1: Think of one reason why the proportion in the sample may not be the same as the proportion of all citizens.
y-m-78-10.s.s1.o.a: 52% came out in the sample and this is greater than 50%, so it's fine to write that it's a majority.
y-m-78-10.s.s1.r.a: You treated the sample proportion of 52% as the same as the proportion of all citizens. The proportion can differ from survey to survey.
y-m-78-10.s.s1.o.b: A margin of error means the survey is inaccurate, so it has no meaning.
y-m-78-10.s.s1.r.b: The interval of 48.9 to 55.1 carries information. It tells us that support is neither very low nor very high.
y-m-78-10.s.s1.o.c: The interval contains 50%, so this survey alone makes it hard to say for sure it is a majority.
y-m-78-10.s.s1.r.c: You decided how strong a conclusion is by whether the interval includes the reference value (50%).
y-m-78-10.s.s1.o.d: If a value is inside the confidence interval, it is equally possible whether it is at the edge or in the middle.
y-m-78-10.s.s1.r.d: Values closer to the middle of the interval tend to be more likely. You can't say the edges are the same.
y-m-78-10.s.s1.explain: The 95% confidence interval is 48.9 to 55.1, so we can't rule out that the support among all citizens is below 50%. It is hard to say for sure 'a majority' from this survey alone.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.prompt: What you have newly learned: when the sample was increased to 4,000 by the same method and surveyed again, 51.6% were in favor, and the 95% confidence interval was about 50.1% to 53.1% (margin of error ±1.5%p). Now, which judgment is fitting?
y-m-78-10.s.s2.hint.0: Write the two intervals side by side and compare how the width (upper end − lower end) changed.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.hint.1: Check with numbers how close the lower end is to 50%.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.o.a: The confidence interval is above 50%, so at the 95% level we can say it is a majority.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.r.a: You judged by comparing the interval with the reference value. This is a statistical reading.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.o.b: The lower end is very close to 50%, so it is a slim majority and other factors must be considered.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.r.b: You added a caution about the statistical judgment.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.o.c: The first survey (52%) and the second survey (51.6%) differ, so neither can be trusted.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.r.c: It is natural for the value to differ a little from survey to survey. The confidence interval reflects that kind of fluctuation.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.o.d: The sample became 4 times larger, so the survey now has no error at all.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.r.d: When the sample gets larger the error gets smaller but does not disappear. A margin of error of ±1.5%p remains.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.explain: The sample got larger so the interval got narrower, and the lower end is 50.1%, barely over 50%. At the 95% level you can say it is a majority, but it is a slim margin, so you should also consider other factors such as the survey method.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.acc.0: The 95% confidence interval is above 50%, so it is statistically valid to say it is a majority at the 95% level. However, it is better to also say that the difference is slim and that factors beyond sampling error remain.
y-m-78-10.s.s3.prompt: A friend says, 'A 95% confidence interval of 48.9 to 55.1 means there is a 95% probability that the proportion in favor among all citizens is in this interval.' Write in one or two sentences how you would refine this explanation, that is, what '95%' means.
y-m-78-10.s.s3.hint.0: Imagine doing the survey 100 times by the same method, and draw the 100 intervals that are made.
y-m-78-10.s.s3.hint.1: Compare the fact that the true proportion for all citizens is one fixed value with the fact that the interval changes from survey to survey.
y-m-78-10.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If you repeat it many times with the same method, ...
y-m-78-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Instead of attaching a probability to a single interval, as in 'the probability of being in this interval', did you explain it as a proportion when the method is used many times?
y-m-78-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you connect '95%' with 'the interval contains the proportion for all'?
y-m-78-10.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say how your explanation differs from your friend's?
y-m-78-10.s.s3.model.0: It means that if you repeat the survey many times by the same method and make intervals, about 95% of the intervals made that way contain the true proportion in favor among all citizens.
y-m-78-10.s.s3.model.1: Whether one interval that has been made contains the true proportion is either right or wrong, and 95% means that when such surveys are repeated again and again, the proportion of intervals that contain the overall proportion is about 95%.
y-m-78-10.s.s3.modelNote.1: This answer moves the object of the probability from 'one interval' to 'the method'.

y-m-78-11.title: They say the test is 90% accurate, so if I test positive, am I 90% likely to be infected?
y-m-78-11.topic: What a positive result means and prevalence (a practical reading of conditional probability)
y-m-78-11.goal: Know that the probability that a positive result means a real infection depends not only on the test's performance but also on the proportion of infected people, and make several cases that fit the conditions.
y-m-78-11.material: A test for a certain infectious disease comes out positive for '90 of 100 infected people' (sensitivity 90%). Minsu tested positive on this test. Minsu thinks, 'The test is 90% accurate, so the probability that I am infected is 90%.' How many infected people there are in the group taking this test, and how many positives come out among people who are not infected, have not yet been revealed.
y-m-78-11.thinking.0: Sorting out the information needed for a judgment
y-m-78-11.thinking.1: Thinking by turning it into concrete numbers like 1000 people
y-m-78-11.thinking.2: Making several cases that satisfy the conditions
y-m-78-11.prereq.0: This task is at the 'H2' difficulty (one step beyond H1) in this platform's production allocation, and it does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this subject to a particular grade. Assume you already know the prerequisite concepts below.
y-m-78-11.prereq.1: How to set the whole as a number like 1000 people and count the people in each part
y-m-78-11.prereq.2: Calculating a ratio (%) as a number of people
y-m-78-11.prereq.3: The meaning of sensitivity (the proportion of positives among infected people) and specificity (the proportion of negatives among non-infected people)
y-m-78-11.s.s1.prompt: To check Minsu's judgment that 'the probability that I am infected is 90%', what more information is needed? Choose everything that is needed.
y-m-78-11.s.s1.hint.0: Write down separately what two kinds of people the people who tested positive are made up of.
y-m-78-11.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what you need to know to find out the size of each kind.
y-m-78-11.s.s1.o.a: The number of people who paid the test fee among those who took this test.
y-m-78-11.s.s1.r.a: The fee has nothing to do with the meaning of the test result.
y-m-78-11.s.s1.o.b: The proportion of actually infected people among those taking this test.
y-m-78-11.s.s1.r.b: In a group where the infected are rare and one where they are common, the same positive means something different.
y-m-78-11.s.s1.r.c: Time has nothing to do with the meaning of the result.
y-m-78-11.s.s1.o.d: The proportion of positives among people who are not infected.
y-m-78-11.s.s1.r.d: How often a positive comes out even though the person is not infected changes the meaning of a positive.
y-m-78-11.s.s1.explain: The people who are positive are a mix of 'positives among the infected' and 'positives among the non-infected'. You need to know the sizes of the two groups (the proportion infected) and the proportion positive among the non-infected to know the proportion of truly infected people among the positives.
y-m-78-11.s.s2.prompt:
The sensitivity is 90%, and 1000 people take the test. The number of infected people is p, and the proportion of negatives among people who are not infected (the specificity) is k%. Decide p and k so that at least half of the positive people are actually infected (positives among infected ≥ positives among non-infected), and enter 3 different combinations.
① p is an integer from 1 to 500
② k is an integer from 90 to 99
③ The number of positives among the infected (0.9×p) is not less than the number of positives among the non-infected ((100−k)%×(1000−p))
y-m-78-11.s.s2.hint.0: Decide on one p, find the number of positives among the infected and the number of non-infected, then change k and see how the number of positives among the non-infected moves.
y-m-78-11.s.s2.hint.1: Compare whether you can raise p when k is low and lower p when k is high.
y-m-78-11.s.s2.ok.c1: p is an integer from 1 to 500.
y-m-78-11.s.s2.fail.c1: p must be an integer from 1 to 500.
y-m-78-11.s.s2.ok.c2: k is an integer from 90 to 99.
y-m-78-11.s.s2.fail.c2: k must be an integer from 90 to 99.
y-m-78-11.s.s2.ok.c3: At least half of the positives are infected.
y-m-78-11.s.s2.fail.c3: Among the people who are positive, the infected are less than half. (You need 90×p ≥ (100−k)×(1000−p))
y-m-78-11.s.s2.explain: If p=20 and k=99, of 20 infected people 18 are positive, and of 980 non-infected people 1%, or 9.8, are positive, so at least half (about 65%) of the positives are infected. Even with the same test, this happens only in a group where the infected are common (p is large) or with a test of high specificity.
y-m-78-11.s.s3.prompt: Think about the case p=20, k=95 (20 infected out of 1000 people, specificity 95%). Explain in one or two sentences to Minsu why, even if he is positive, the probability of being infected may be much lower than 90%.
y-m-78-11.s.s3.hint.0: Divide the 1000 people into infected and non-infected, and write how many in each are positive.
y-m-78-11.s.s3.hint.1: Count how many of all the positive people are infected.
y-m-78-11.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The infected are ... while the non-infected ...
y-m-78-11.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you compare the number of positives among the non-infected (about 49) with the number of positives among the infected (18)?
y-m-78-11.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say which kind of people most of the positives come from?
y-m-78-11.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you explain it not as 'the test is bad' but as 'it changes because of the makeup of the group'?
y-m-78-11.s.s3.model.0: There are only 20 infected people out of 1000, so 90% of them, 18, are positive. On the other hand, 5% of the 980 who are not infected, about 49, also come out positive. Of the roughly 67 positives, only 18 are infected, so the probability is about 27%.
y-m-78-11.s.s3.model.1: It is not because the test is wrong, but because there are far more people who are not infected. When even 5% of the healthy 980 become positive, the people who become positive by error (about 49) outnumber the positives from the infected (18), so even if you are positive, the probability of being infected is low.
y-m-78-11.s.s3.modelNote.1: This answer explains it by comparing numbers.

y-m-78-12.title: How should we set the mean and standard deviation so that defects are around 5%?
y-m-78-12.topic: Designing a specification using the roughly 95% interval of a normal distribution
y-m-78-12.goal: Using the property that about 95% falls within 2 standard deviations around the mean, interpret the conditions on the mean and standard deviation of a production process, and choose one among several solutions and state its risk.
y-m-78-12.material: At a snack factory, assume the weight (g) of one bag follows a normal distribution with mean μ ('mu') and standard deviation σ ('sigma'). The specification is 95 g or more and 107 g or less, and a bag outside the specification is defective. Using the rule that about 95% of bags fall within 2 standard deviations of the mean (μ−2σ to μ+2σ), we take it that for defects to be about 5% or less, this interval must lie inside the specification.
y-m-78-12.thinking.0: Turning a rule into conditions and finding several solutions
y-m-78-12.thinking.1: Sorting out whether a setting satisfies the conditions
y-m-78-12.thinking.2: Saying how to check the assumption (normal distribution)

y-m-78-12.s.s2.prompt:
Find 3 different settings of (mean μ, standard deviation σ) that fit the factory's requirements, and enter them.
① μ−2σ ≥ 95 and μ+2σ ≤ 107 (defects about 5% or less)
② The mean is at least the labeled weight of 100 g (μ ≥ 100)
③ The standard deviation is at least 1 g (σ ≥ 1, because it costs a lot to control more precisely)
y-m-78-12.s.s2.hint.0: First decide on a mean, and find the distances from that mean to the lower and upper limits of the specification.
y-m-78-12.s.s2.hint.1: Think about how the shorter of the two distances sets the maximum of the standard deviation.
y-m-78-12.s.s2.ok.c1: The interval of 2 standard deviations around the mean is inside the specification.
y-m-78-12.s.s2.fail.c1: The interval μ−2σ to μ+2σ goes outside the specification of 95 to 107 g.
y-m-78-12.s.s2.ok.c2: The mean is at least 100 g.
y-m-78-12.s.s2.fail.c2: The mean must be at least 100 g.
y-m-78-12.s.s2.ok.c3: The standard deviation is at least 1 g.
y-m-78-12.s.s2.fail.c3: The standard deviation must be at least 1 g.
y-m-78-12.s.s2.explain: There are very many settings that satisfy the conditions. For example, (100, 2): 96 to 104 g, (101, 2.5): 96 to 106 g, (102, 2): 98 to 106 g. The closer the mean is to the middle of the specification (101 g), the larger you can make the standard deviation.
